title: Mass Spectrometry Bacterial Classification
body:
For a graduate-level machine learning course (CS5841), my team and I investigated whether modern deep learning could improve on classical machine learning approaches for identifying bacterial species from MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry data — a task clinical labs rely on for fast microbial diagnosis.

I wrote the initial versions of the data pipeline and modeling code, directed model selection, and wrote the Data & Analysis and Results sections of the paper. We compared a feed-forward network, a convolutional neural network, and an attention-based architecture across 20 bacterial species, using log1p-scaled spectra and stratified 5-fold cross-validation to handle a fairly small and imbalanced dataset (651 samples).

Somewhat counterintuitively, the simplest model won: a two-layer feed-forward network reached 95.0% cross-validation accuracy and 92.4% accuracy on the held-out test set, edging out both the CNN (94.2%) and the attention-based model (92.5%). We found the more complex architectures were more prone to memorizing the small training set, and that Leaky ReLU activations consistently outperformed standard ReLU across all three model types.
